strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: the 'frozen world' assumption in LRM evaluation, motivated by real deployment scenarios such as long-running coding agents.

Provides a clean formalization of interruption (hard/soft time-constrained and update-driven) with well-defined metrics (interruption-conditioned accuracy, output length), which gives the community a reusable evaluation framework.

Identifies and clearly characterizes three concrete, interesting failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) with quantitative prevalence estimates and illustrative qualitative examples, adding genuine new understanding of LRM behavior beyond prior efficient-reasoning literature.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: multiple math and coding benchmarks, multiple interrupt positions, three models of different design (Qwen3, GPT-OSS, Magistral), plus scaling ablations and assistant-turn vs. user-turn comparisons.
Proposes and evaluates a simple mitigation (prompt guidance) that meaningfully improves robustness to update-driven interruptions on easier tasks, offering actionable insight for practitioners.
Releases dataset/code and documents dataset construction and prompts in detail, aiding reproducibility.
Honest limitations section acknowledging domain narrowness, single-event interruption assumption, and small model set.
weaknesses: Model selection is limited to relatively small/mid-sized open-weight models (8B, 20B, 24B); no frontier proprietary reasoning models (e.g., o1/o3, Gemini, full-size DeepSeek-R1) are tested, which are precisely the models motivating the paper's opening example of hours-long reasoning, limiting the generalizability of conclusions.

Interruption is simulated post-hoc by truncating a fully generated trace rather than intervening during actual generation in a live/streaming setting; this may not fully capture how a model would behave if it anticipated interruption, and the framing of 'X as a fraction of the full trace' requires knowing the full trace length in advance, which is not realistic in deployment.

Most benchmarks are evaluated with a single run (except AIME with 16 trials), so accuracy differences and failure-mode rates may be subject to sampling noise not fully captured by the reported confidence intervals.

Definitions/detection of failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) appear to rely on heuristic or qualitative judgment (e.g., length thresholds, keyword patterns) rather than a rigorously validated automatic classifier with inter-rater reliability, which weakens the precision of the quantitative claims (e.g., '90% of errors due to panic').

The update-driven dataset construction relies heavily on GPT-5 generation with manual verification by the authors only; there is limited discussion of annotator agreement, error rates in the augmentation process, or whether verification was blind, raising some concern about dataset quality/bias.

The 'prompt guidance' fix is a fairly shallow prompt-engineering patch (telling the model the update is verified) rather than a principled solution, and the paper does not explore why self-doubt occurs mechanistically or test more robust mitigations (e.g., fine-tuning).

The headline '60% drop' and other extreme statistics appear to be drawn from specific late-interruption conditions on hard benchmarks (e.g., AIME) and may overstate the generality of the fragility across all settings/tasks.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: the 'frozen world' assumption in LRM evaluation, which is genuinely relevant as reasoning traces grow longer and agentic coding workflows become common.
Provides a reasonably clean formalization of three interruption regimes (hard, soft, update-driven) with well-defined metrics (interruption-conditioned accuracy and length).
The qualitative failure-mode taxonomy (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) is intuitive and illustrated with concrete, convincing transcripts that make the phenomena easy to understand.
Includes a public dataset/benchmark and a fairly detailed (if imperfect) description of the augmentation pipeline for update-driven interrupts, as well as scaling ablations across model sizes.
Explores a simple mitigation ('prompt guidance') and shows it has a measurable, if partial, effect, pointing toward an actionable direction for future work.
weaknesses: Model coverage is narrow and not representative of the motivating use case: all experiments use three small-to-mid-size open models (8B, 20B, 24B); no frontier/long-horizon reasoning models (e.g., o1/o3, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek-R1 itself) are evaluated, despite the introduction explicitly motivating the work with hours-long agentic coding sessions from such systems. This substantially limits the significance and generalizability of the claims.

The 'interruption' protocol is not a live/streaming intervention but a post-hoc simulation: the full reasoning trace is generated first and then truncated at a fixed fraction of its final length. This requires oracle knowledge of the eventual trace length and may not faithfully represent what happens with a true real-time interrupt, especially for the open-ended, variable-length generations models actually produce when truly cut off mid-stream.

The update-driven dataset is constructed largely via GPT-5 generation with only coarse 'manual verification by the authors' and no reported inter-annotator agreement, error rates, or independent validation protocol — raising concerns about silent biases or artifacts in the augmented benchmark that the headline numbers depend on.

Key quantitative claims about failure-mode prevalence (e.g., '90% of new errors are panic', '80% of errors are self-doubt') are not accompanied by a clear, reproducible automatic detection/classification methodology; it is unclear how these categories were operationalized beyond manual case inspection, undermining reproducibility of the central qualitative findings.

The paper's chosen injection mechanism (interrupting within the assistant/thinking turn rather than a new user turn) is explicitly justified by format-following failures of the tested models rather than by what realistic deployed systems do; the authors acknowledge user-turn interruption is 'more natural' but relegate it to an ablation, meaning the main results may be partly an artifact of an atypical intervention protocol rather than a property of interruptibility per se.

Statistical rigor is uneven: only AIME uses repeated trials (16) with bootstrapped CIs; GSM8K, MATH500, and LiveCodeBench results are single-run, which is a weak basis for the many fine-grained comparisons (across 5 interrupt positions, 3 models, multiple settings) presented in the figures.

The proposed mitigation ('prompt guidance') is an ad hoc prompt-engineering patch (explicitly telling the model, in its own voice, that the update is 'verified') rather than a principled fix, and its benefits are inconsistent (still large gaps on AIME/LiveCodeBench), so the paper stops short of offering a real solution to the problems it identifies.

Overall the contribution is primarily an evaluation/benchmark paper with limited methodological novelty beyond combining existing ideas (budget forcing, missing-premise overthinking) into a new scenario; given the narrow model set and protocol concerns, the significance of the empirical conclusions for the broader claim that 'LRMs are not interruptible' is weaker than the framing suggests.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem framing: the paper convincingly argues that the standard 'frozen world' static evaluation paradigm for LRMs is unrealistic for long-running reasoning tasks (e.g., assistive programming), and proposes a clean, general formalization (hard/soft/update-driven interruptions) with well-defined evaluation metrics (interruption-conditioned accuracy and length).

Comprehensive empirical study spanning math (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25) and coding (LiveCodeBench-v6) benchmarks, three diverse open models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-S-1.2), and multiple interruption types/positions, giving a fairly thorough picture of the phenomenon.

Identification and detailed qualitative illustration of three distinct, previously under-characterized failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt), each supported with concrete transcripts in the appendix, which is useful for the community and could inspire future training/mitigation work.

Useful ablations: model-scale analysis (1.7B/8B/32B) reveals interesting non-monotonic effects (e.g., reasoning leakage increasing in smaller models via post-hoc reasoning), and assistant-turn vs. user-turn comparisons probe the sensitivity of findings to intervention locus.

Practical mitigation ('prompt guidance') is proposed and empirically shown to substantially reduce self-doubt failures on easier benchmarks, demonstrating the problem is at least partially addressable without retraining.
Reasonably strong reproducibility support: detailed prompts, dataset construction pipeline (including human verification), and stated intent to release code/dataset/project page.
weaknesses: The model pool is narrow and does not include any frontier closed models (e.g., o1/o3, Gemini, DeepSeek-R1) that are prominently cited in the introduction as motivating examples, which limits the generality of claims framed as being about 'state-of-the-art LRMs' and makes it unclear whether findings transfer to the most capable systems actually used in the motivating scenarios.

The interruption protocol defines cut points as fractions of a pre-computed, full (uninterrupted) reasoning trace obtained via a separate oracle run; this is a somewhat artificial construct since in real deployments the eventual trace length is unknown a priori and models are not aware interruption may occur at a specific relative point, raising some construct-validity concerns about how closely this simulates real interactive use.

The quantitative attribution of errors to specific failure modes (e.g., '90% of new errors from panic', '~80% of update errors from self-doubt', reported prominently in the abstract and Figure 1) is not clearly described methodologically in the main text — it is unclear whether these rates come from automated heuristics, length/pattern-based classifiers, or manual annotation, and no inter-rater or validation statistics are given, which limits reproducibility of these specific headline numbers.

Update-driven dataset construction relies on GPT-5 generated augmentations with verification only by the paper's own authors; no inter-annotator agreement, error rates, or independent quality audit are reported, leaving open the possibility of systematic artifacts or biases in the augmented problems that could affect measured update-driven degradation.

The study is restricted to single, well-defined interruption/update events in math and code domains; the authors acknowledge (appropriately) that real interruptions may be noisy, adversarial, or multi-turn, and that other domains (dialogue, planning, collaborative writing) are not covered, which somewhat limits the breadth of the claimed contribution despite being honestly disclosed as a limitation.

Presentation is figure-heavy with dense multi-panel plots that are sometimes difficult to parse quickly, and some figures (e.g., Figures 2, 3, 6) pack a large amount of information per panel without sufficient in-text walk-through, which could hinder accessibility for readers less familiar with the setup.

strengths: Novel and practically important problem formulation: the paper challenges the pervasive 'frozen world' assumption in LRM evaluation, introducing formalized protocols for hard/soft time-constrained interruptions and update-driven interruptions, which is a fresh and timely angle not well studied in prior efficient-reasoning or budget-forcing literature.

Extensive empirical scope: experiments span multiple open-weight model families (Qwen3, GPT-OSS, Magistral, DeepSeek-R1-Llama, Nemotron) across multiple sizes, and multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME-24/25, LiveCodeBench-v6), with substantial appendix material (scaling studies, absolute-token binning, sentence-level granularity, user-turn vs assistant-turn ablations, Chain-of-Draft baseline) that stress-tests the robustness of the main findings.

Identification of three concrete, well-illustrated and seemingly novel failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) with qualitative examples, quantitative prevalence measurements, and a sensible mitigation (prompt guidance) demonstrating the taxonomy has actionable value.

Careful methodological safeguards: human verification of the augmented update-driven dataset, benchmark-memorization control experiment (running augmented problems without updates to check models aren't just recalling originals), and human validation of the panic/self-doubt classifiers with reported agreement rates.

Good transparency and reproducibility efforts: detailed prompts, dataset construction pipeline, and code/dataset release are provided, along with an honest limitations section and disclosure of LLM usage in writing.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to open-weight models under simulated single-turn interruptions; closed-source frontier models (which are most widely deployed) are only approximated via a rough GPT-5.4-Mini proxy that the authors themselves say is 'substantially below native reasoning capability,' limiting the generalizability of claims about SOTA LRMs.

The panic and self-doubt classifications rely on heuristics (e.g., <1% remaining context threshold) and an LLM-based classifier (GPT-5) rather than fully rigorous, model-agnostic definitions; although human agreement rates (88-90%) are reported, these are based on small samples (50 examples) and could still embed subjective judgment calls that affect the reported prevalence statistics.

The single, well-defined, pre-specified interruption point setup (vs. noisy/adversarial/multiple interruptions in real deployments) and the single-round (non-agentic) scope, while reasonably justified, mean the ecological validity of findings for real multi-turn/agentic use cases remains an open and somewhat speculative extrapolation, despite the authors' claim that findings 'should generalize.'

The core contribution is diagnostic rather than solution-oriented; the one proposed mitigation (prompt guidance) is a simple, ad hoc engineered postfix that only partially helps (largely on easy tasks), so the practical takeaway for practitioners beyond 'this is a real problem' is somewhat limited.

Some presentation issues: the large number of similar-looking figures across main text and extensive appendix makes it hard to track key comparative numbers at a glance, and certain analyses (e.g., dataset augmentation quality, exact statistical test details for 'no significant difference' claims in paraphrase ablation) could be described more rigorously/quantitatively rather than qualitatively.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant and under-explored question — how LRMs behave when the 'frozen world' assumption is violated by interruptions or mid-reasoning updates — and formalizes it with a clean notation (interruption-conditioned accuracy, length metrics) that could serve as a template for future work.

Extensive empirical coverage: five model families, four benchmarks, multiple interrupt types (hard, soft, update-driven), several ablations (model scale, assistant- vs user-turn, prompt paraphrase, absolute- vs relative-position binning, Chain-of-Draft baseline), and an appendix with substantial additional experiments.

The identified failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) are intuitive, well-illustrated with qualitative examples, and the authors provide some quantitative robustness checks (e.g., panic-threshold sensitivity analysis, human agreement rates with LLM-based self-doubt classifier) rather than relying purely on anecdote.

The dataset construction methodology (augmenting GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/LiveCodeBench with human-verified updates, with a memorization-control check) is reasonably careful, and the authors release code/data.
weaknesses: The contribution is almost entirely diagnostic: no new training method, architecture, or principled mitigation is proposed. The one 'fix' offered (a hand-crafted 'prompt guidance' postfix) is a narrow, ad-hoc prompt-engineering trick tuned to the authors' own injection format, and even the authors concede it does not meaningfully help on harder tasks (AIME, LiveCodeBench) or weaker models (DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B). This limits the paper's lasting usefulness beyond a benchmark release.

Several key behavioral definitions rely on brittle heuristics rather than principled measurement: 'panic' is defined as closing thinking after using <1% of remaining context (an arbitrary threshold, even though sensitivity analysis is reported), and 'self-doubt' is detected via an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5) with only 88% human agreement on a 50-sample check — a small and potentially non-representative validation set for a core claim of the paper.

The interruption/update injection protocol is highly artificial and synthetic: interruption tokens, update tags, and system prompts explicitly prime the model to expect updates in a fixed <update> format. This is quite different from how interruptions would actually arise in deployed, naturalistic interactive settings (e.g., via API turn-taking), so the measured failure rates may not transfer to real usage, and the paper's own ablation (Sec 6.2) shows user-turn interruptions behave differently/worse, raising concern about how representative the main assistant-turn protocol is.

No closed-source frontier models (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude) are evaluated under native interruption; the GPT-5.4-Mini 'proxy' explicitly disables real reasoning and is acknowledged by the authors as 'substantially below the model's native reasoning capability,' making the central claim that 'even state-of-the-art LRMs' fail under interruption largely untested for genuinely state-of-the-art systems.

The scope is restricted to single-turn math and coding tasks with one synthetic interruption per trace; the generalization claim to multi-turn, agentic, or tool-using settings (explicitly the most realistic and motivating use case in the introduction, e.g. 'a coding model needs to work in an environment where other models are modifying the same codebase') is asserted but never tested, which is a significant gap given that the motivating examples throughout the paper are agentic/collaborative scenarios.

The dataset augmentation pipeline depends heavily on GPT-5 generation with author-only verification (no independent/blind annotators, no inter-annotator agreement reported for the update dataset itself, only for the failure-mode classifiers), raising reproducibility and potential bias concerns for a benchmark intended for community reuse.

Numerous ablations are reported but mostly confirm the main findings qualitatively rather than adding new insight or stress-testing the core claims against alternative explanations (e.g., whether the observed accuracy drops are simply explainable by reduced token budget alone rather than qualitatively distinct 'pathologies').

Presentation issues: the main text is dense with many cross-referenced figures split between main paper and a very long appendix, making the core claims harder to verify without extensive appendix-diving; some figures (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 6) pack many subplots with small text that are hard to parse.

strengths: Challenges a widely-held but rarely-questioned assumption (the 'frozen world' assumption) in LRM evaluation, and does so with a clear, well-motivated formalization of interruption scenarios (hard/soft time-constrained and update-driven), making the problem setting precise via the M(q,r:X,i) notation.

Extensive empirical coverage: five open-weight model families, four benchmarks spanning math and code, multiple interruption positions, several granularities of interruption (character/sentence/absolute-token), both relative and absolute-length re-binning analyses, and a model-scaling study, all of which substantially strengthen robustness of the core claims.

Identification and careful characterization of three distinct, named failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) that are intuitive, reproducible across models, and supported by both quantitative metrics and qualitative transcripts (Appendix C), giving the taxonomy explanatory and diagnostic value for the community.

Methodologically careful validation efforts: human agreement checks for the panic heuristic (sensitivity across thresholds, 90% human agreement) and the LLM-based self-doubt classifier (88% human agreement), plus a memorization check for the update-driven dataset construction showing models do not trivially recall original answers.

Simple, training-free mitigation (prompt guidance) is tested and shown to meaningfully help on easier tasks while honestly reporting its limits on harder tasks (AIME, LiveCodeBench), plus a paraphrase-invariance ablation and comparison with an existing efficient-reasoning baseline (Chain of Draft), showing the pathologies are not merely artifacts of a specific prompt or method.

Transparent and thorough documentation: full prompts, dataset construction pipeline, and code/data release support reproducibility; limitations section is candid about scope (math/coding only, single pre-specified interrupt, open-weight models only, no proposed training fix).
weaknesses: The interruption protocol inserts synthetic control tokens/instructions directly into the assistant's reasoning stream (e.g., appending `<update>` tags or 'I have received an update...' text), which is an artificial mechanism not necessarily representative of how real interactive systems or APIs would deliver interruptions; the paper acknowledges this (Sec. 6.2) but it still limits ecological validity of the main findings.

Evaluation is restricted to math and coding tasks with single, well-defined interruption events; no evaluation on agentic, tool-use, or multi-turn dynamic settings where interruptions are arguably most practically relevant, despite the motivating examples in the introduction referencing exactly these settings (e.g., collaborative coding environments).

Closed-source/frontier models (GPT-5.2, Gemini 3, etc.) cannot be evaluated under the true protocol since APIs don't expose reasoning traces for intervention; the GPT-5.4-Mini proxy is explicitly flagged as not faithful, leaving open whether the most capable deployed models exhibit the same severity of pathologies.

The prompt-guidance mitigation, while interesting, is a fairly narrow intervention (appending model-voiced affirmation text) and its substantial variance in effectiveness across tasks (near-complete fix on GSM8K/MATH500 vs. limited benefit on AIME/LiveCodeBench, and Qwen3 remaining fragile) suggests the underlying cause of self-doubt is not well understood mechanistically, leaving the analysis largely descriptive rather than explanatory.

The 'panic' and 'self-doubt' classifiers rely on heuristics (1% remaining-context threshold) and an LLM-judge, respectively; although sensitivity/agreement checks are reported, these are based on small samples (50 examples) and the thresholds/classifiers could still introduce some labeling noise into the headline statistics (e.g., 'up to 80% of performance loss attributable to panic').

Dataset augmentation for update-driven interruptions relies on GPT-5 generation with author-only manual verification (no independent/external annotation or inter-annotator agreement reported), which could introduce subtle construction biases despite the reported 80% acceptance rate without changes.
